claims.evidence: Supported by the experimental data and Figures 3B, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claims.claim: Gene Ontology term analysis showed that the overall functional assignments for excitatory, inhibitory, and motor clusters were similar in the adult human spinal cord.
claims.source: We found that the overall functional assignments for excitatory, inhibitory, and motor clusters were similar in the adult human spinal cord (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), such as chemical or glutamatergic synaptic transmission, axon guidance, neuron projection development, glutamate receptor signaling pathway, regulation of NMDA receptor activity, and ion transmembrane transport, suggesting that these neuronal subpopulations cooperated in the regulation of spinal functions.
claims.evidence: Supported by the Gene Ontology analysis and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Excitatory and inhibitory neurons were predominantly mapped to the dorsal horn.
claims.source: Excitatory (Figure 3F) and inhibitory (Figure 3G) neurons were predominantly mapped to the dorsal horn, which was confirmed by IF staining of their markers.
claims.evidence: Supported by the spatial mapping data and immunofluorescence staining shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claims.claim: Motor neurons (CHAT positive) were predominantly located in the ventral horn, with scattered expression in the dorsal horn.
claims.source: Motor neurons (CHAT positive) were predominantly located in the ventral horn, with scattered expression in the dorsal horn (Figure 3H), which is consistent with the recent published study (Yadav et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by the spatial mapping data shown in Figure 3H and citation to published literature (Yadav et al., 2023).

claims.claim: Gene set variation analysis indicated that C3, C4, C6, C7, C8, C10, and C13–19 clusters were predominantly present in the superficial dorsal horn; C1, C2, and C12 clusters were in the deep dorsal horn, C5, C9, and C11 clusters were present across the superficial and deep dorsal horn, while C0 and C20 clusters were mainly located in the ventral horn.
claims.source: For specific clusters, gene set variation analysis (GSVA) indicated that C3, C4, C6, C7, C8, C10, and C13–19 clusters were predominantly present in the SD; C1, C2, and C12 clusters were in the DD, C5, C9, and C11 clusters were present across the SD and the DD, while C0 and C20 clusters were mainly located in the ventral horn (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by the gene set variation analysis and Figures 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: C8 was mapped to the superficial dorsal horn, and its representative marker, PDYN (prodynorphin), was distributed primarily in laminae I–II.
claims.source: For example, C8 was mapped to the superficial dorsal horn, and its representative marker, PDYN (prodynorphin, ligands for the kappa-type of opioid receptor), was distributed primarily in laminae I–II (Figure 3J), consistent with the previously reported location of PDYN-expressing neurons in the rodent spinal cord (Duan et al., 2014; Sapio et al., 2020; Serafin et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by the spatial mapping data and immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 3J, and citations to published literature (Duan et al., 2014; Sapio et al., 2020; Serafin et al., 2019).

claims.claim: CCK (cholecystokinin) was widely present in human dorsal glutamatergic neurons, consistent with the findings in mice.
claims.source: For instance, CCK (cholecystokinin, involved in sensory processing under physiological and pain conditions) (Liu et al., 2018; Peirs et al., 2021; Figure 3—figure supplement 6A–D) and SST (somatostatin, involved in transmitting itch and pain sensation) (Fatima et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Figure 3—figure supplement 6E–H) were widely present in human dorsal glutamatergic neurons, consistent with the findings in mice (Todd, 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by the immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6A–D and citations to published literature (Liu et al., 2018; Peirs et al., 2021; Todd, 2017).

claims.claim: SST (somatostatin) was widely present in human dorsal glutamatergic neurons, consistent with the findings in mice.
claims.source: For instance, CCK (cholecystokinin, involved in sensory processing under physiological and pain conditions) (Liu et al., 2018; Peirs et al., 2021; Figure 3—figure supplement 6A–D) and SST (somatostatin, involved in transmitting itch and pain sensation) (Fatima et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Figure 3—figure supplement 6E–H) were widely present in human dorsal glutamatergic neurons, consistent with the findings in mice (Todd, 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by the immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6E–H and citations to published literature (Fatima et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Todd, 2017).

claims.claim: FOXP2 (Forkhead box P2) was presented in both human glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons.
claims.source: FOXP2 (Forkhead box P2, involved neuronal differentiation and movement disorders) (Rousso et al., 2012) was presented in both human glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 6I–L).
claims.evidence: Supported by the immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6I–L and citation to published literature (Rousso et al., 2012).

claims.claim: The neuronal data of the human spinal cord overlapped well with those from the mouse in the uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP).
claims.source: Overall, the neuronal data of the human spinal cord overlapped well with those from the mouse in the uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis and Figure 4A showing the coclustering of mouse and human neurons.

claims.claim: Homologous clusters between humans and mice showed a highly similar transcriptional profile.
claims.source: To more directly compare the single-nucleus RNA-seq data from human and mouse spinal cord, homologous clusters between humans and mice were identified (Figure 4B) using the methods as previously described (Nguyen et al., 2021), which showed a highly similar transcriptional profile between species (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis and Figures 4B and 4C, and citation to published literature (Nguyen et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Shared representative genes for several homologous neuronal clusters in humans and mice include ZFHX3 or Zfhx3 for C2, SOX5 or Sox5 for C4, and GRM3 or Grm3 for C9.
claims.source: We found shared representative genes for several homologous neuronal clusters in humans and mice, such as ZFHX3 or Zfhx3 (zinc finger homeobox 3) for C2, SOX5 or Sox5 (SRY-box transcription factor 5) for C4, and GRM3 or Grm3 (glutamate receptor, metabotropic 3) for C9.
claims.evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis of gene expression between human and mouse data.

claims.claim: The transcriptional patterns were similar between human and mouse spinal cords for several genes, including CHRM3 or Chrm3, NRXN3 or Nrxn3, NXPH1 or Nhpx1, DSCAML1 or Dscaml1, CACNA2D3 or Cacna2d3, and GRIK1 or Grik1 predominantly expressed in inhibitory clusters.
claims.source: The transcriptional patterns were similar between human and mouse spinal cords, such as CHRM3 or Chrm3 (cholinergic receptor muscarinic 3), NRXN3 or Nrxn3 (neurexin 3), NXPH1 or Nhpx1 (neurexophilin 1), DSCAML1 or Dscaml1 (DS cell adhesion molecule like 1), CACNA2D3 or Cacna2d3 (calcium voltage-gated channel auxiliary subunit alpha 2 delta 3), and GRIK1 or Grik1 (glutamate ionotropic receptor kainate type subunit 1) were predominantly expressed in inhibitory clusters, and CACNA2D1 or Cacna2d1 (calcium voltage-gated channel auxiliary subunit alpha 2 delta 1), EBF1 or Ebf1 (EBF transcription factor 1), EBF2 or Ebf2 (EBF transcription factor 2), CPNE4 or Cpne4 (copine 4), CPNE8 or Cpne8 (copine 8), MAML3 or Maml3 (mastermind like transcriptional coactivator 3), PDE11A or Pde11a (phosphodiesterase 11A), SOX5 or Sox5 (SRY-box transcription factor 5), and ERBB4 or Erbb4 (erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 4) were predominantly expressed in excitatory clusters.
claims.evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis of gene expression between human and mouse data.

claims.claim: CACNA2D1 or Cacna2d1, EBF1 or Ebf1, EBF2 or Ebf2, CPNE4 or Cpne4, CPNE8 or Cpne8, MAML3 or Maml3, PDE11A or Pde11a, SOX5 or Sox5, and ERBB4 or Erbb4 were predominantly expressed in excitatory clusters in both human and mouse spinal cords.
claims.source: The transcriptional patterns were similar between human and mouse spinal cords, such as CHRM3 or Chrm3 (cholinergic receptor muscarinic 3), NRXN3 or Nrxn3 (neurexin 3), NXPH1 or Nhpx1 (neurexophilin 1), DSCAML1 or Dscaml1 (DS cell adhesion molecule like 1), CACNA2D3 or Cacna2d3 (calcium voltage-gated channel auxiliary subunit alpha 2 delta 3), and GRIK1 or Grik1 (glutamate ionotropic receptor kainate type subunit 1) were predominantly expressed in inhibitory clusters, and CACNA2D1 or Cacna2d1 (calcium voltage-gated channel auxiliary subunit alpha 2 delta 1), EBF1 or Ebf1 (EBF transcription factor 1), EBF2 or Ebf2 (EBF transcription factor 2), CPNE4 or Cpne4 (copine 4), CPNE8 or Cpne8 (copine 8), MAML3 or Maml3 (mastermind like transcriptional coactivator 3), PDE11A or Pde11a (phosphodiesterase 11A), SOX5 or Sox5 (SRY-box transcription factor 5), and ERBB4 or Erbb4 (erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 4) were predominantly expressed in excitatory clusters.
claims.evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis of gene expression between human and mouse data.

claims.claim: SLC5A7 or Slc5a7, SLIT3 or Slit3, CREB5 or Creb5, and PRUNE2 or Prune2 were predominantly expressed in motor neurons in both human and mouse spinal cords.
claims.source: SLC5A7 or Slc5a7 (solute carrier family 5 member 7), SLIT3 or Slit3 (slit guidance ligand 3), CREB5 or Creb5 (cAMP responsive element binding protein 5), and PRUNE2 or Prune2 (prune homolog 2) were predominantly expressed in motor neurons.
claims.evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis of gene expression between human and mouse data.

claims.claim: Differential expression between excitatory and inhibitory neurons was observed for a pair of calcium channels (CACNA2D1 or Cacna2d1, and CACNA2D3 or Cacna2d3) in humans and mice.
claims.source: As expected, genes associated with neurotransmitter status were identified (such as GAD1, Gad2, Slc6a1, Chat, SLC5A7, and Slc5a7), but we also observed differential expression between excitatory and inhibitory neurons for a pair of calcium channels (CACNA2D1 or Cacna2d1, and CACNA2D3 or Cacna2d3) in humans and mice.
claims.evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis of gene expression between human and mouse data.

claims.claim: The findings regarding differential expression of calcium channels were consistent with a previous study.
claims.source: These findings were consistent with a previous study (Russ et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Russ et al., 2021).

claims.claim: The expression of SST was significantly higher in C13 than in other clusters of humans.
claims.source: For example, the expression of SST was significantly higher in C13 than in other clusters of humans (Figure 4D and F), and the expression of NPY (neuropeptide Y, which influences many physiological processes, such as cortical excitability and stress response) was higher in C11 than in other clusters of humans (Figure 4D and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claims.claim: The expression of NPY (neuropeptide Y) was higher in C11 than in other clusters of humans.
claims.source: For example, the expression of SST was significantly higher in C13 than in other clusters of humans (Figure 4D and F), and the expression of NPY (neuropeptide Y, which influences many physiological processes, such as cortical excitability and stress response) was higher in C11 than in other clusters of humans (Figure 4D and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claims.claim: In the mouse spinal cord, Nts (neurotensin) showed selectively higher expression levels in C13.
claims.source: In the mouse spinal cord, Nts (neurotensin that may function as a neurotransmitter or a neuromodulator) and Nos1 (nitric oxide synthase 1 that functions as a neurotransmitter) showed selectively higher expression levels in C13 and C8, respectively (Figure 4E and G).
claims.evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4E and 4G.

claims.claim: In the mouse spinal cord, Nos1 (nitric oxide synthase 1) showed selectively higher expression levels in C8.
claims.source: In the mouse spinal cord, Nts (neurotensin that may function as a neurotransmitter or a neuromodulator) and Nos1 (nitric oxide synthase 1 that functions as a neurotransmitter) showed selectively higher expression levels in C13 and C8, respectively (Figure 4E and G).
claims.evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4E and 4G.

claims.claim: TAC1 (tachykinin precursor 1) and NPY were mainly present in the clusters of superficial dorsal neurons of both human and mouse spinal cord.
claims.source: For example, TAC1 (tachykinin precursor 1, functions as a neurotransmitter) and NPY were mainly present in the clusters (e.g., C4 and C11, respectively) of superficial dorsal neurons of both human (Figure 4D and F) and mouse spinal cord (Figure 4E and G), which were confirmed by RNAscope ISH and/or IF staining (Figure 4H–K).
claims.evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D, 4E, 4F, and 4G, and RNAscope ISH and IF staining shown in Figures 4H–K.

claims.claim: Calca (calcitonin-related polypeptide alpha) was selectively expressed in C20 of mice.
claims.source: For example, Calca (calcitonin-related polypeptide alpha, which is involved in migraine) was selectively expressed in C20 of mice (Figure 4E and G), but CALCA almost did not exist in human spinal neurons (Figure 4D and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D, 4E, 4F, and 4G.

claims.claim: CALCA almost did not exist in human spinal neurons.
claims.source: For example, Calca (calcitonin-related polypeptide alpha, which is involved in migraine) was selectively expressed in C20 of mice (Figure 4E and G), but CALCA almost did not exist in human spinal neurons (Figure 4D and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claims.claim: GRP (gastrin releasing peptide) was predominantly present in C7 of humans.
claims.source: GRP (gastrin releasing peptide) was predominantly present in C7 of humans (Figure 4D and F), but Grp showed little expression in all mouse spinal neuronal clusters (Figure 4E and G).
claims.evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claims.claim: Grp showed little expression in all mouse spinal neuronal clusters.
claims.source: GRP (gastrin releasing peptide) was predominantly present in C7 of humans (Figure 4D and F), but Grp showed little expression in all mouse spinal neuronal clusters (Figure 4E and G).
claims.evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4E and 4G.

claims.claim: Several genes, such as PAM, OPRM1, EBF1, GABRG3, GRIK2, SCN1A, KCND2, and RORA, were highly and widely expressed in the spinal neurons of both humans and mice.
claims.source: Of note, several genes, such as PAM (peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase), OPRM1 (opioid receptor mu 1), EBF1, GABRG3 (gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptor subunit gamma3), GRIK2 (glutamate ionotropic receptor kainate type subunit 2), SCN1A (sodium voltage-gated channel alpha subunit 1), KCND2 (potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily D member 2), and RORA (RAR related orphan receptor A), were highly and widely expressed in the spinal neurons of both humans and mice (Figure 4D and G, Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3), which may provide some guidance for future studies that focus translational efforts on conserved molecular targets across species.
claims.evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D, 4G, and Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claims.claim: Several genes, such as CALCA, GAL, and NPR1, showed little expression in the human spinal cord.
claims.source: However, several genes, such as CALCA, GAL (galanin), and NPR1 (natriuretic peptide receptor 1), showed little expression in the human spinal cord (Figure 4D and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 3J–L), which should be considered during clinical translation.
claims.evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D, 4F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3J–L.

claims.claim: Neuronal barcodes from both sexes were represented in all subclusters, suggesting that males and females have the same spinal neuronal subtypes.
claims.source: Neuronal barcodes from both sexes were represented in all subclusters, suggesting that males and females have the same spinal neuronal subtypes (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Supported by the sex difference analysis and Figure 5A showing barcodes from males and females in all clusters.

claims.claim: The comparative results showed similar gene expression profiles between male and female spinal neuronal clusters, except for C20 (motor neurons).
claims.source: The comparative results showed similar gene expression profiles between male and female spinal neuronal clusters (Figure 5B), except for C20 (motor neurons) (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Supported by the sex difference analysis and Figures 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: C20 (motor neurons) had the highest number of differentially expressed genes between males and females.
claims.source: C20 (motor neurons) had the highest number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (Figure 5C), suggesting potential molecular differences in mechanisms of motor function between men and women.
claims.evidence: Supported by the sex difference analysis and Figure 5C.

claims.claim: In C20 (motor neurons), males showed higher expression of genes that encode potassium channels and lower expression of genes that encode sodium channels compared to females.
claims.source: A main finding in C20 was the higher expression of genes that encode potassium channels, whereas a lower expression of genes that encode sodium channels was found in males compared to females (Figure 5D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by the sex difference analysis and Figures 5D and 5E.

claims.claim: The finding of higher expression of genes encoding potassium channels and lower expression of genes encoding sodium channels in males compared to females in C20 was validated by immunofluorescence staining examining SCN10A expression in CHAT neurons from male and female donors.
claims.source: This finding was validated in IF staining examining SCN10A (sodium voltage-gated channel alpha subunit 10) expression in CHAT neurons from male and female donors (Figure 5F and G).
claims.evidence: Supported by the immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figures 5F and 5G.

claims.claim: Other genes encoding proteins associated with pain sensation were differentially expressed in C20 between male and female donors, such as HCN1, FGF13, LRFN5, HTR2C, and KCNQ3.
claims.source: In addition, other genes encoding proteins associated with pain sensation were differentially expressed in C20 between male and female donors (Figure 5E), such as HCN1 (hyperpolarization activated cyclic nucleotide gated potassium channel 1) (He et al., 2019; Santoro and Shah, 2020), FGF13 (fibroblast growth factor 13) (Wang et al., 2021b), LRFN5 (leucine-rich repeat and fibronectin type III domain containing 5) (Johnston et al., 2019), HTR2C (5-hydroxytryptamine receptor 2C) (Mickey et al., 2012), and KCNQ3 (potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily Q member 3) (Palomés-Borrajo et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by the sex difference analysis shown in Figure 5E and citations to published literature (He et al., 2019; Santoro and Shah, 2020; Wang et al., 2021b; Johnston et al., 2019; Mickey et al., 2012; Palomés-Borrajo et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Gene Ontology term analysis of differentially expressed genes between males and females showed that upregulated genes in males were associated with pathways implicated in neurotransmitter secretion, synaptic transmission, axon guidance, exocytosis, and neuron project development.
claims.source: GO term analysis of DEGs between males and females showed that upregulated genes in males were associated with pathways implicated in neurotransmitter secretion, synaptic transmission, axon guidance, exocytosis, and neuron project development (Figure 5H), while downregulated genes in males were associated with pathways implicated in response to heat, neuron apoptotic process, RNA splicing, and protein catabolic process (Figure 5I).
claims.evidence: Supported by the Gene Ontology analysis and Figure 5H.

claims.claim: Gene Ontology term analysis of differentially expressed genes between males and females showed that downregulated genes in males were associated with pathways implicated in response to heat, neuron apoptotic process, RNA splicing, and protein catabolic process.
claims.source: GO term analysis of DEGs between males and females showed that upregulated genes in males were associated with pathways implicated in neurotransmitter secretion, synaptic transmission, axon guidance, exocytosis, and neuron project development (Figure 5H), while downregulated genes in males were associated with pathways implicated in response to heat, neuron apoptotic process, RNA splicing, and protein catabolic process (Figure 5I).
claims.evidence: Supported by the Gene Ontology analysis and Figure 5I.

claims.claim: Spatial transcriptomics was performed on the L3-5 DRGs from the same six adult donors as in the spinal cord.
claims.source: We also performed spatial transcriptomics on the L3-5 DRGs from the same six adult donors as in the spinal cord (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Supported by the experimental methods described and Figure 6A showing the workflow.

claims.claim: DRG cells were initially classified into 16 clusters.
claims.source: DRG cells were initially classified into 16 clusters (Figure 6B), which were categorized into six major populations based on their distinct transcriptional characteristics (Figure 6C and D), including fibroblasts, immune cells, red blood cells (RBCs), Schwann cells, a mixed population of vascular endothelial cells (VECs)/vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and a mixed population of neurons and satellite glial cells (SGCs) (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Supported by the experimental data and Figure 6B showing the UMAP plot of 16 cell types.

claims.claim: The 16 DRG cell clusters were categorized into six major populations: fibroblasts, immune cells, red blood cells (RBCs), Schwann cells, a mixed population of vascular endothelial cells (VECs)/vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and a mixed population of neurons and satellite glial cells (SGCs).
claims.source: DRG cells were initially classified into 16 clusters (Figure 6B), which were categorized into six major populations based on their distinct transcriptional characteristics (Figure 6C and D), including fibroblasts, immune cells, red blood cells (RBCs), Schwann cells, a mixed population of vascular endothelial cells (VECs)/vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and a mixed population of neurons and satellite glial cells (SGCs) (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Supported by the experimental data and Figures 6C, 6D, and 6E.

claims.claim: Neurons and their surrounding satellite glial cells (SGCs) could not be completely separated in the DRG spatial transcriptomics data.
claims.source: As expected, neurons and their surrounding SGCs could not be completely separated (Figure 6E and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by the technical limitations of the spatial transcriptomics method and Figures 6E and 6F.

claims.claim: Each individual donor contributed nuclei to each cluster and no individual donor was responsible for any specific cluster in the DRG spatial transcriptomics data.
claims.source: We verified that each individual donor contributed nuclei to each cluster and that no individual donor was responsible for any specific cluster (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by the verification described and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: DRG neurons were classified into 13 subclusters: peptidergic neurons (PEP1-6), nonpeptidergic neurons (NP1-2), and neurofilament neurons (NF1-5).
claims.source: To determine the heterogeneity within DRG neurons, we further classified them into 13 subclusters: peptidergic neurons (PEP1-6), nonpeptidergic neurons (NP1-2), and neurofilament neurons (NF1-5) (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) based on well-known representative marker genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by the experimental data and Figure 7A showing the UMAP plot of 13 neuronal clusters.

claims.claim: The findings indicate a similar transcriptional pattern of DRG neurons between humans and mice.
claims.source: Consistent with previous studies (Nguyen et al., 2021; Tavares-Ferreira et al., 2022), our findings indicate a similar transcriptional pattern of DRG neurons between humans and mice.
claims.evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis and citations to published literature (Nguyen et al., 2021; Tavares-Ferreira et al., 2022).

claims.claim: Sst-positive neurons represent a distinct subcluster in mouse DRG, but SST is widely expressed across different DRG subclusters in humans.
claims.source: For example, Sst-positive neurons represent a distinct subcluster in mouse DRG (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 3B), but SST is widely expressed across different DRG subclusters in humans (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis and Figures 7D, 7E, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: Th-positive cells represent a distinct subcluster in mouse DRG, but TH was almost not present in human spinal neurons.
claims.source: Th-positive cells represent a distinct subcluster in mouse DRG (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 3B), but TH was almost not present in human spinal neurons (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis and Figures 7D, 7E, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: PVALB is widely expressed in different subclusters of human DRG but shows very low expression in mouse DRG.
claims.source: PVALB is widely expressed in different subclusters of human DRG (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 3A) but shows very low expression in mouse DRG (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis and Figures 7D, 7E, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: Gpx3 is selectively expressed in the mouse PEP1 cluster, but GPX3 exhibits high expression in multiple human DRG subclusters.

results.result: Spatial transcriptomics of human spinal cord identified 17 cell types that were classified into five major clusters: neurons, Schwann cells, a mixed population of neurons and astrocytes, a mixed population of meningeal and vascular cells, and a mixed population of glial cells. Due to the lower resolution of spatial transcriptomics, neurons were not well separated from surrounding astrocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21 describe the spatial transcriptomics workflow, initial identification of 17 cell types, their classification into 5 major clusters, and technical limitations. The data are supported by appropriate figures (1A-G) showing UMAP plots, marker gene expression, and spatial distribution. The technical limitation regarding neuron-astrocyte separation (C20) is appropriately acknowledged and consistent with known spatial transcriptomics resolution constraints.

results.result: Single-nucleus RNA-seq of 64,021 nuclei from nine human donors identified eight major cell types with distinct spatial distributions: oligodendrocytes (58.8%), microglia (13.1%), neurons (11.9%), astrocytes (5.2%), OPCs (4.6%), vascular cells (3%), meningeal cells (2.1%), and Schwann cells (1.2%). Neurons were predominantly in gray matter, while oligodendrocytes and microglia were mainly in white matter.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C28 present the single-nucleus RNA-seq results with appropriate sample sizes (n=9 donors, 64,021 nuclei), cell type identification with percentages, gene detection rates, and spatial validation by IF staining. The data are well-supported by Figures 2A-F and supplementary figures. Quality control verification showing each donor contributed to each cluster (C24) strengthens confidence in the results.

results.result: Human spinal cord neurons were classified into 21 subclusters based on transcriptional characteristics and neurotransmitter status: 11 excitatory (54.4%), 8 inhibitory (34.5%), 1 mixed (9.6%), and 1 motor neuron cluster (1.5%). Spatial mapping and gene set variation analysis revealed distinct distributions across superficial dorsal horn, deep dorsal horn, and ventral horn, validated by immunofluorescence staining of marker genes including PDYN, CCK, SST, and FOXP2.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C38 describe the neuronal subclassification with appropriate methodology (transcriptional characteristics, neurotransmitter markers), spatial localization using GSVA, and validation by IF staining. The results are supported by comprehensive figures (3A-J, supplementary figures) showing UMAP plots, marker expression, spatial distribution, and IF validation. The consistency with published literature (citations to Yadav et al., 2023; Todd, 2017) adds credibility.

results.result: Comparison of human and mouse spinal cord neurons revealed overall similarity in transcriptional profiles with homologous clusters showing highly similar gene expression patterns. Shared representative genes were identified across species, including ZFHX3 for C2, SOX5 for C4, and differential expression of calcium channels (CACNA2D1 in excitatory, CACNA2D3 in inhibitory neurons) was conserved between species.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C46 present cross-species comparison using appropriate integration methods (Seurat anchoring, homology mapping). The results are supported by Figures 4A-C showing UMAP coclustering and heatmaps of conserved gene expression. The identification of shared marker genes and conserved differential expression patterns (e.g., calcium channels) is well-documented and consistent with prior literature (Russ et al., 2021).

results.result: Transcriptional profiling of classical spinal cord markers revealed both conserved and divergent expression patterns between human and mouse. While genes like TAC1 and NPY showed similar expression in superficial dorsal neurons across species, species-specific differences were observed: CALCA was selectively expressed in mouse C20 but nearly absent in human neurons, while GRP was predominantly in human C7 but showed little expression in mouse. Several genes (PAM, OPRM1, EBF1, GABRG3, GRIK2, SCN1A, KCND2, RORA) were highly expressed in both species.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C57 describe differential and conserved gene expression patterns across species, supported by dot plots and heatmaps (Figures 4D-K, supplementary figures). The validation by RNAscope ISH and IF staining (C51) strengthens the findings. The identification of both conserved targets for translation and species-specific differences is important for clinical translation considerations.

results.result: Sex difference analysis revealed that males and females have the same spinal neuronal subtypes, with similar gene expression profiles across most clusters except motor neurons (C20). In motor neurons, males showed higher expression of potassium channel genes and lower expression of sodium channel genes compared to females, validated by IF staining of SCN10A. Additional pain-related genes (HCN1, FGF13, LRFN5, HTR2C, KCNQ3) were differentially expressed in motor neurons between sexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C65 present sex difference analysis with appropriate statistical criteria (FC ≥ 1.33, adjusted p<0.05) and validation by IF staining (Figures 5F-G). The finding of sex-specific differences primarily in motor neurons (C20) is well-supported by volcano plots, violin plots, and GO term analysis. The validation of SCN10A expression differences by quantitative IF analysis adds rigor. However, the functional implications of these differences remain speculative.

results.result: Spatial transcriptomics of human DRG from six donors identified 16 cell clusters categorized into six major populations: fibroblasts, immune cells, RBCs, Schwann cells, VECs/VSMCs, and neurons/SGCs. Due to technical limitations, neurons and surrounding satellite glial cells could not be completely separated.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C70 describe DRG spatial transcriptomics with appropriate methodology and acknowledgment of technical limitations. The results are supported by Figures 6A-F showing workflow, UMAP plots, and marker gene expression. The verification that each donor contributed to each cluster (C70) demonstrates data quality. The acknowledged limitation of neuron-SGC separation (C69) is consistent with spatial transcriptomics resolution constraints.

results.result: DRG neurons were classified into 13 subclusters: peptidergic (PEP1-6), nonpeptidergic (NP1-2), and neurofilament neurons (NF1-5), with functional annotations including nociceptors, proprioceptors, and LTMRs. Comparison with mouse DRG revealed overall similarity but notable differences: SST was widely expressed across human DRG subclusters but represented a distinct subcluster in mice; PVALB was widely expressed in human but showed low expression in mouse; TH was present in mouse but nearly absent in human DRG.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C82 present DRG neuronal classification with appropriate marker genes and functional annotations consistent with published literature (Tavares-Ferreira et al., 2022). The cross-species comparison is supported by dot plots and heatmaps (Figures 7A-G, supplementary figures), with validation by RNAscope ISH and IF staining (C82). The identification of species-specific expression patterns is well-documented and important for translational research.

results.result: Ligand-receptor interaction analysis between DRG and spinal cord neurons revealed putative connections including: CALCA-CALCRL (DRG to spinal C16), NGF-NGFR (DRG to spinal C0 and C16), SST-SSTR1 (DRG to spinal C6, C8, C19), APOE-LRP1 (DRG to spinal C6, C8, C10, C12), SLIT2-ROBO2 (NF4 to multiple spinal clusters), TAC1-TACR1 (PEP2-4 to dorsal spinal clusters), and NRG1-ERBB4 (NF clusters to superficial dorsal horn).
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C89 present ligand-receptor interaction analysis using appropriate computational methods (SingleCellSignalR). The results are supported by Figure 8A-H showing interaction networks and spatial localization. While the interactions are computationally predicted and represent putative connections, the methodology is appropriate and the results are consistent with known biology (e.g., NRG1-ERBB4 interactions supported by citations to Calvo et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2022).

results.result: IL4R, IL31RA, and IL13RA1 (type 2 inflammatory cytokine receptors) were more widely expressed across human DRG neuron subtypes than in mice. Additionally, PVALB and SST showed broader expression across human DRG neuronal clusters than in mice, suggesting genes are more selectively expressed in mice than in human DRGs.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C130 describe species differences in inflammatory cytokine receptor and marker gene expression, supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 4 and consistent with previous studies (Jung et al., 2023; Tavares-Ferreira et al., 2022). The inference that genes are more selectively expressed in mice (C130) is reasonable based on the observed broader expression patterns in humans, though this represents a generalization from limited examples.

results.result: NRG1 from NF clusters (myelinated DRG neurons) is paired with ERBB4 in spinal superficial dorsal horn clusters, consistent with previous studies. This suggests NRG1 is likely secreted by NF clusters, activates ERBB4+ neurons in the superficial dorsal horn, and may induce heat hypersensitivity. NGFR and CALCRL in spinal C16 received broad inputs from various DRG neuronal clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C138 present ligand-receptor pairing data (C136, supported by Figure 8H and citations) but make mechanistic inferences about NRG1 secretion and heat hypersensitivity (C137) and functional importance of C16 (C138) that go beyond the computational predictions. While consistent with prior literature (Wang et al., 2022; Calvo et al., 2010), these functional claims require experimental validation (e.g., functional assays, perturbation experiments) that are not provided.

results.result: Prior work has established the cellular composition and heterogeneity of the spinal cord, the advantages of single-nucleus RNA sequencing, and previous studies in mouse and developing human spinal cord. However, limited research has defined neuronal heterogeneity and spatial distribution in the adult human spinal cord at single-cell resolution, which is important because findings from animal experiments cannot always be directly replicated in humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C12 summarize prior work and establish the rationale for the current study. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to published literature. The gap in knowledge regarding adult human spinal cord (C11) and the challenge of translating animal findings to humans (C12) provide clear justification for the study.

results.result: This study classified human spinal cord neurons into 21 subtypes with distinct transcriptional patterns, molecular markers, and functional annotations. The overall molecular and cellular organization is similar to mice with some heterogeneity. Several genes showed sex differences in motor neurons, and a publicly available website was created for data exploration.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 summarize the main findings of the study, which are supported by the detailed results presented in subsequent claims and figures. The creation of a publicly available website (C16) enhances the impact and accessibility of the resource.

results.result: Discussion of prior work on pain prevalence, sex differences, spinal cord function, and comparison with recent studies (Yadav et al., 2023) showing consistent findings regarding cell type distribution and marker gene expression. Species differences were noted, including the classification of cholinergic clusters as independent in human but part of excitatory clusters in mouse, and differences in expression patterns of opioid peptide genes (PENK, PDYN).
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C112 provide context from prior literature and compare current findings with recent work (Yadav et al., 2023). The claims are well-supported by appropriate citations and the comparisons with Yadav et al. demonstrate consistency in major findings while highlighting specific differences. The discussion of species differences in cholinergic cluster classification (C106-C107) and opioid peptide expression (C111-C112) is supported by the data.

results.result: Discussion of prior work on DRG heterogeneity in rodents and humans, noting that multiple studies have characterized human DRG neurons with varying nomenclatures and cluster definitions. Previous studies identified genes differentially expressed between human and mouse DRG, including broader expression of SCN4B, IL31RA, IL4R, IL10RA, IL13RA1, TRPV1, SCN8A, and CALCA in human compared to mouse. Inconsistent nomenclatures across studies hinder comparison and clinical translation.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C127 summarize prior work on DRG characterization and highlight the challenge of inconsistent nomenclatures across studies (C124). All claims are supported by appropriate citations. The discussion of species differences in gene expression (C125-C126) and the role of inflammatory cytokines (C127) provides important context for the current findings.

results.result: Discussion of prior work on DRG-spinal cord connections, noting that dorsal spinal neurons receive different DRG primary afferents to process sensory information, and that primary afferent axons terminate in different laminae. Previous studies showed NRG1 is mainly produced in myelinated neurons and that DRG TRPV1+ neuron-spinal ErbB4+ neuron connections are involved in heat sensation.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C135 provide context from prior literature on DRG-spinal cord connectivity and NRG1-ERBB4 signaling. All claims are supported by appropriate citations (Todd, 2010; Todd, 2017; Wang et al., 2022; Calvo et al., 2010; Velanac et al., 2012; Willem et al., 2006). This context supports the interpretation of the ligand-receptor interaction analysis.

results.result: Methods: Lumbar spinal cord and L3-5 DRGs were isolated from nine adult brain-dead human donors (6 males, 3 females, 35-59 years old) within 90 minutes of cross-clamping. Donors had no acute/chronic pain and died from cerebral hernia or intraventricular hemorrhage. All procedures were approved by appropriate ethics committees and informed consent was obtained.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C143 describe the sample collection and ethical procedures. The methods are appropriate with clear inclusion/exclusion criteria, rapid tissue collection (within 90 min), and proper ethical approvals. The sample size (n=9 donors) is reasonable for this type of study, though larger samples would strengthen statistical power for sex difference analyses.

results.result: The authors used 10x Genomics Visium spatial transcriptomics on lumbar spinal cord from six adult human donors and identified 17 cellular types, which were classified into five major clusters. Due to the lower resolution of Visium, neurons were not well separated from surrounding astrocytes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the authors' efforts to address Visium limitations by complementing spatial data with snRNA-seq from the same tissue. One reviewer noted 'the authors made considerable efforts to acknowledge and objectively address the limitations of Visium while attempting to overcome them by utilizing single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) from the same tissue.' The technical limitation regarding cell separation was recognized but not criticized as a flaw.

results.result: Single-nucleus RNA-seq was performed on 64,021 nuclei from nine adult human donors, identifying eight major cell types with distinct spatial distributions. Neurons were mainly in gray matter, oligodendrocytes and microglia in white matter, and astrocytes widely distributed but more highly expressed in white matter.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recognized this as a valuable contribution. One reviewer stated 'This study offers a thorough exploration of both cellular and spatial heterogeneity within the human spinal cord. The resulting atlas datasets and analysis findings represent valuable resources for the neuroscience community.' The spatial mapping and validation with immunofluorescence were not questioned.

results.result: Human spinal cord neurons were classified into 21 subclusters based on transcriptional characteristics and neurotransmitter status: 11 excitatory (glutamatergic), 8 inhibitory (GABAergic/glycinergic), 1 mixed, and 1 motor neuron cluster. These showed distinct spatial distributions with excitatory and inhibitory neurons predominantly in the dorsal horn and motor neurons in the ventral horn.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged this classification as valuable. One reviewer noted 'The manuscript provides a valuable database for the molecular and cellular organization of adult human spinal cords in addition to published datasets (Andersen, et al. 2023; Yadav, et al. 2023).' The spatial localization findings were consistent with recent publications and were not challenged.

results.result: Comparison between human and mouse spinal cord neurons showed overall similar transcriptional profiles with highly similar homologous clusters, but some species-specific differences in gene expression patterns. Several genes showed conserved expression patterns while others (e.g., CALCA, GRP) showed species-specific differences.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the comparative analysis but noted limited novelty. One reviewer stated 'despite the extensive bioinformatics-based analyses performed, the results mostly confirm what has been previously reported (Nguyen et al. 2021; Yadav et al. 2023; Jung et al. 2023).' The findings were accepted as valid but not particularly novel.

results.result: Sex difference analysis showed that males and females have the same spinal neuronal subtypes, but C20 (motor neurons) had the highest number of differentially expressed genes between sexes. Males showed higher expression of potassium channel genes and lower expression of sodium channel genes compared to females, validated by immunofluorescence for SCN10A.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised significant concerns about the validation and quantitative rigor of sex difference findings. One reviewer noted 'The authors reported that SCN10A, associated with nociceptos, exhibited stronger expression in females. While they intend to validate this finding through IF, the quantitative difference is not clearly observed in the IF data (Figure 5f). It would be essential to provide validation through DAPI-based cell counts.' Another reviewer stated 'the assertions regarding the sex differences in motor neurons...appear preliminary and necessitate more rigorous validation.'

results.result: Spatial transcriptomics on L3-5 DRGs from six donors identified 16 clusters categorized into six major populations, with neurons further classified into 13 subclusters (peptidergic, nonpeptidergic, and neurofilament neurons). Due to Visium limitations, neurons and satellite glial cells could not be completely separated.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about the lack of snRNA-seq validation for DRG findings. One reviewer stated 'The study did not perform snRNA-seq in the DRG. The limitations of Visium in cell type separation are acknowledged, and the authors are aware that Visium alone has limitations in describing cell expression patterns. The authors need to validate their findings via analyses of public DRG snRNA-seq data (Jung et al. 2023 Ncom; Nguyen et al. 2021eLife) before drawing broad conclusions.' Another noted 'Figure 7's comparison between human Visium spot data and Renthal et al.'s mouse snRNA-seq may have limitations as Visium spot data could not provide a transcriptional profile at the single cell resolution.'

results.result: Comparison between human and mouse DRG neurons showed similar transcriptional patterns overall, but with notable species-specific differences. SST, TH, PVALB, and GPX3 showed different expression patterns between species, with broader expression across human DRG clusters. IL4R, IL31RA, and IL13RA1 were more widely expressed in human DRG than in mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged these findings as consistent with previous studies. One reviewer noted the value of demonstrating 'the expression of these itch receptors in DRG' in response to recent findings about type 2 cytokines. The validation with RNAscope ISH and IF staining was accepted without criticism.

results.result: Ligand-receptor interaction analysis revealed potential communication between DRG and spinal cord neurons, including CALCA-CALCRL, NGF-NGFR, SST-SSTR1, APOE-LRP1, SLIT2-ROBO, TAC1-TACR1, and NRG1-ERBB4 pairs. NRG1 from myelinated DRG neurons paired with ERBB4 in spinal superficial dorsal horn.
results.evaluation: Reviewers indicated that the interaction analysis was preliminary and lacked sufficient depth. One reviewer stated 'the assertions regarding...the potential interactions between DRG and spinal cord neuronal subclusters appear preliminary and necessitate more rigorous validation.' Another requested 'more comprehensive analyses of potential interaction based on distance should be provided, beyond the top 10 interactions (Figure 8)' noting that 'juxtacrine and paracrine signals operate from 0 to 200 um, spatial information is vital to understanding intercellular communication.'

results.result: The study classified human spinal cord neurons into 21 subtypes with distinct transcriptional patterns, molecular markers, and functional annotations. The overall molecular and cellular organization was similar to mice with some heterogeneity. A publicly available website was created for data access.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the value of the atlas and database. One stated 'The manuscript provides a valuable database for the molecular and cellular organization of adult human spinal cords in addition to published datasets.' Another noted 'The resulting atlas datasets and analysis findings represent valuable resources for the neuroscience community.' However, concerns were raised about the 'largely observational approach and lack of quantitative analysis.'

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate spatial transcriptomics workflow and cell type identification (C17-C21) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes appropriate figures and technical acknowledgments. Peer reviewers commend the authors for addressing Visium limitations with complementary snRNA-seq data and do not criticize the technical limitations as flaws.

Both evaluate snRNA-seq results (C22-C28) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights appropriate sample sizes, quality control, and validation. Peer reviewers recognize this as a valuable contribution to the neuroscience community, with no concerns raised about the methodology or validation.

Both evaluate neuronal subclassification (C29-C35 overlap) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval covers C29-C38 with comprehensive validation. Peer reviewers acknowledge the classification as valuable and consistent with recent publications, with no challenges to the spatial localization findings.

Both address cross-species comparison (C39-C46 in OpenEval; C39-C57 in peer review) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval finds the integration methods and conserved patterns well-documented. Peer reviewers accept the findings as valid but note limited novelty, stating results mostly confirm previous reports.

Both evaluate differential gene expression patterns (C47-C57). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with validation by RNAscope and IF. Peer reviewers also rate as SUPPORTED but emphasize limited novelty, noting the results confirm previously reported findings.

Both evaluate sex difference analysis (C58-C65) but with different conclusions. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED while noting functional implications remain speculative. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, raising significant concerns about validation rigor and quantitative differences in IF data, requesting DAPI-based cell counts.

Both address DRG spatial transcriptomics (C66-C70 overlap). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with appropriate acknowledgment of limitations. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, expressing concern about lack of snRNA-seq validation and requesting validation via public DRG snRNA-seq datasets before drawing broad conclusions.

Both evaluate DRG neuronal classification (C71-C76 overlap). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED (C71-C82) with appropriate validation. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, concerned about comparing Visium spot data with mouse snRNA-seq due to resolution limitations.

Both address DRG neuronal markers and species differences (C77-C82 overlap). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with validation by RNAscope and IF. Peer reviewers also rate as SUPPORTED, acknowledging findings as consistent with previous studies and accepting the validation without criticism.

Both evaluate ligand-receptor interaction analysis (C83-C89 overlap). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting computational predictions are appropriate and consistent with known biology. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, stating assertions appear preliminary and requesting more comprehensive spatial-based analyses beyond top 10 interactions.

Both address species differences in inflammatory markers (C128-C129 overlap). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, finding the inference reasonable based on observed patterns. Peer reviewers also acknowledge these findings as consistent with previous studies regarding itch receptors in DRG.

Both evaluate NRG1-ERBB4 interactions and functional claims (C136-C138). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting mechanistic inferences go beyond computational predictions and require experimental validation. Peer reviewers also rate as UNCERTAIN, stating assertions about DRG-spinal cord interactions are preliminary and need more rigorous validation.

Both evaluate the study's main findings and atlas contribution (C13-C16) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the support from detailed results and public accessibility. Peer reviewers acknowledge the valuable database and resources but raise concerns about the largely observational approach and lack of quantitative analysis.
